title: Photography direction for a creative studio
excerpt: Choose photographs that show one decision in the work, and caption them. A reel with no explanation is a mood, not an argument.
alt: A long, quiet office corridor with glass rooms, a teal sofa, and a dark kitchen, a room that cannot stand in for the work itself.
caption: A quiet office corridor with glass rooms, a teal sofa, and a dark kitchen. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a portfolio photograph prove?
faqs.answer: One decision. Crop to the type, the grid, or the space you defended, and caption the choice. A desk, a plant, and a distant laptop can be pleasant and still leave the buyer unsure what you did.

faqs.question: When is a reel acceptable?
faqs.answer: After a sentence and a still, on a project page, where the visitor chooses to play it. The still should already contain the decision. Autoplay on the homepage spends the first seconds on atmosphere.

faqs.question: What should alt text say?
faqs.answer: What is actually in the frame, written so someone who cannot see the image still learns the fact. A single word such as screenshot is not enough. Do not put a search phrase in the alt if it is not in the picture.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Creative studio website photography should show one decision in the work. Reject a reel with no explanation. The pictures are part of the argument, not a mood pasted under the headline.

A client who has already seen fifty portfolios can enjoy a beautiful frame and still learn nothing. Beauty without a decision is the house style of the sites they forgot. Your frames have to be usable as evidence.

## Pictures are part of the argument

Decide the sentence before you choose the frame. "We cut the grid so the material could be read." "We set the archive in type a reader can stay with." "We kept the store familiar while the platform changed." Then pick the photograph that makes that sentence visible. If no photograph can make it visible, the sentence is still abstract, or you are showing the wrong artifact.

Put the picture next to the sentence, not in a separate band called "gallery." A band of images with no lines under them is a reel that learned to sit still. The buyer will scroll it the way they scroll a social feed, which is to say they will feel something and remember nothing you can be hired for.

Crop is the edit. Show the part that holds the choice. A full homepage at a distance, inside a laptop mockup, on a desk, beside a plant, is four frames of delay. The plant is not the decision. The type, the grid, or the empty space you defended is the decision. Get closer.

Sequence is the edit too. One establishing frame so they know what the object is. One close frame so they can see the choice. Stop. A third frame only if it shows a different choice, such as the phone version of a layout you refused to shrink blindly. More than that and you are performing abundance.

## Show the decision, not the studio

The client hired a judgment, not a tour of your chairs. A portrait of the team can belong on the about page, small, next to the jobs those people do. It should not lead the homepage if the homepage's job is the work. A brick wall, a skylight, and a pour-over are pleasant and interchangeable. Fifty studios have them. They do not prove you can choose.

When you do show people, show them in the act that matters. A review of a printed page. A hand marking a crop. Two people looking at the same screen with the work visible, not with the back of the laptop toward the camera. If the screen is a blur of color, you photographed a meeting, not a decision.

Work-in-progress can be honest if it is labeled. A wall of printed screens with string between them is a planning picture. It supports a sentence about how you connect a flow. It does not support a sentence about the finished site unless the finished site is also on the page. Do not let process photos stand in for the result. Clients have been shown process as a way to avoid showing the thing.

Public projects are a useful standard. Thomas Bewick needs pictures of reading, type, and the archive, not of a moodboard. Down the Cove needs the store, the product, the path to buy. Wabisabi needs material and crop. Ballarat Box Sports needs the community it is for. If your photograph could be swapped with another studio's and the caption would still "work," the photograph is not evidence.

## Reject the unexplained reel

A reel fails this buyer when it is a sequence of taste with no sentence. Autoplay makes it worse. The page starts an argument the visitor did not consent to, often with motion they cannot pause, often under a headline that says nothing the film does not already gesture at. You have used the first ten seconds on atmosphere.

If a film is truly the best proof, put it behind a sentence and a still. Let them choose to play it. The still should already contain the decision, so the film is a deeper look, not the only look. Write a caption a person could read with the sound off. If the caption is "a glimpse into our process," you do not have a caption.

Do not use a reel to hide weak projects. Four seconds of each piece, graded to match, is how uneven work pretends to be a body. This client has seen the trick. They will ask which frame they can open. If the answer is none, the reel was a lock on the proof.

Music is almost never worth it. It dates, it clashes with the office they are sitting in, and it says the pictures needed help. Let the work be quiet. Quiet is a kind of confidence, and it respects people who browse with sound they did not ask for.

## Crop, sequence, and caption

Write the caption as a fact about the picture and a fact about the decision. "The product page after the grid was cut to the pieces that share a material." Not "so fresh, so us." The caption is where a skimming buyer learns what you did. [Nielsen Norman Group's research](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) found that people read only about a quarter of the text on a page they actually open. The caption may be the fraction. Spend it on the choice.

Keep a small set of crops and stick to them. Full bleed for one hero that can carry a sentence. A contained image for evidence in the middle of a paragraph. A detail for the thing you want them to inspect. Mixing every ratio you own makes the page feel like a folder. Folders are not direction.

Color and grade should not do the brand's job by force. If every project is pushed through the same heavy grade, you are hiding the work inside the studio's filter. A light, consistent treatment is enough so the site feels like one place. The project's own color has to survive. Otherwise the portfolio is a lookbook of your preset.

Art direction includes what you refuse to retouch. Do not rebuild a project's interface in the photograph so it looks cleaner than production. The buyer who opens the live site and finds a different grid will trust you less, not more. Photograph the real thing, or show a design frame and label it as a design frame.

## Alt text is part of the direction

Every image needs a text alternative that says what is in the frame. [The W3C's WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) puts this under perceivable content. A person who cannot see the picture, and a person on a slow connection who has not received it yet, should still get the fact. "Screenshot" is not a fact. "Laptop" is not a fact. "Homepage of the archive, with the search field and a single engraving on a quiet grid" is a fact.

Write the alt with the caption, not in a bulk rename the night before launch. If you cannot describe the picture without saying "abstract visual of our ethos," the picture is not carrying an argument. Replace it. Alt text is a cheap test of whether the direction is real.

Do not stuff the alt with the phrase you hope to rank for. The alt describes the photograph. The article, or the case study, can say what the studio does in the sentence beside it. A keyword in the alt that is not in the picture is a false description. It fails the visitor and it fails the point of the field.

Decorative marks, if you truly need them, can be hidden from assistive tech. Almost nothing on a proof page is decorative. If it is, ask why it is on a proof page.

## A shot list small enough to finish

Before a launch, write a list you can actually shoot or export. For each proof page: one frame of the decision, one detail, one picture of the context only if the context is the constraint. For the homepage: the single frame that matches the opening sentence. For the about page: the people, if you are naming them, in a place that looks like the real studio, not a rented loft you will never use again.

- Export the interface at the crop you designed, from the real build when you can.
- Photograph materials only when material is the decision.
- Skip the handshake, the laptop-from-behind, and the night skyline.
- Caption each file in the same pass, while you still remember what the choice was.

Store the selects where the client can find them later. On a Hanabi project, brand files and final images live in the client portal with the docs and the updates, so the direction does not collapse into a chat thread. Your studio needs some version of that habit. A shot list with no home becomes a folder named Final-v7.

Direction is a set of rules you can hand to the next person who adds a page. If the rules are "make it feel premium," you do not have direction. If the rules are "show the decision, caption it, describe the frame," you do.

The frames also have to work on the device the buyer is holding. A crop that only reads on a wide monitor will fail the visit you are most likely to get. [The mobile visit for a creative studio](/blog/the-mobile-visit-for-a-creative-studio) is the next piece to write. The first screen still has to show one decision and a way to start a project, and the photograph has to survive that width.

When you want the site's pictures held to the same line as the interface, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring the sentence you want the hero to prove, and the frames you are unsure about. The useful outcome is a shorter shot list, not a moodier grade.
